Lectio Continua
LEK-tsee-oh kon-TIN-yoo-uh
n. phrase (Latin; preaching method)
Latin lectio (reading; the reading of Scripture) + continua (continuous, unbroken, going through). The practice of reading or preaching through a biblical book continuously, passage by passage in canonical order, until the whole book is completed—the Reformation's recovery of the synagogue and early church practice of sequential biblical proclamation.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Lectio continua is the method of preaching or reading through a biblical book in continuous canonical sequence—beginning at chapter one and proceeding verse by verse until the book is complete, then moving to the next. It stands in deliberate contrast to the medieval lectionary system, which assembled selected pericopes for liturgical seasons and often left whole books of Scripture unpreached for years. The synagogue practice modeled something close to it: “And he came to Nazareth, where He had been brought up. And as was His custom, He entered the synagogue on the Sabbath, and stood up to read” (Luke 4:16)—continuous synagogue Torah readings through the year. Ezra and the Levites demonstrated expository reading: “they read from the book, from the law of God, translating to give the sense so that they understood the reading” (Neh 8:8). Paul charges Timothy: “Until I come, give your attention to the public reading, to exhortation, and to teaching” (1 Tim 4:13)—public reading that presupposed orderly, extended engagement with the text. The Reformation recovery was championed by Ulrich Zwingli, who on January 1, 1519, began preaching through the Gospel of Matthew at the Grossmünster in Zurich. Calvin continued the method in Geneva, preaching through Job, Acts, the Pauline epistles, and the Psalms, filling years with whole books. The method submits the preacher to the whole counsel of God (Acts 20:27) rather than allowing him to select comfortable or crowd-pleasing texts.

Webster 1828 Definition

The Reformation recovery of continuous, sequential preaching through whole books of the Bible—from Zwingli at Zurich (1519) and Calvin at Geneva, submitting preacher and congregation alike to the whole counsel of God rather than a curated lectionary.

LECTIO CONTINUA, n. phrase (Latin). The practice of reading or preaching through a biblical book in continuous sequence, verse by verse, until it is completed—the Reformation's primary homiletical method.

Distinguished from the medieval lectio selecta: the lectionary chose pericopes for liturgical seasons, often leaving whole books and difficult texts unread for generations. The lectio continua forces the preacher into territory the lectionary would never choose.

The synagogue background (Luke 4:16–20; Acts 13:14–15) shows continuous Torah readings as the Jewish norm; Ezra's model (Neh 8:8) adds the element of explanation and sense-giving that marks expository lectio continua.

Zwingli inaugurated the Reformation form on New Year's Day 1519, preaching through Matthew at the Grossmünster. Calvin was the master practitioner: his Genevan sermons on Job (159 sermons), Acts (189 sermons), and the Pauline epistles extended over years of continuous exposition.

The homiletical discipline: the preacher who commits to lectio continua cannot avoid the hard texts, cannot skip the inconvenient passages, and cannot shape the congregation's diet around personal preference. The text sets the agenda; the preacher follows.

Key Scripture

Luke 4:16 — "And He came to Nazareth, where He had been brought up. And as was His custom, He entered the synagogue on the Sabbath, and stood up to read."

Nehemiah 8:8 — "And they read from the book, from the law of God, translating to give the sense so that they understood the reading."

1 Timothy 4:13 — "Until I come, give your attention to the public reading, to exhortation, and to teaching."

Acts 2:42 — "They were continually devoting themselves to the apostles' teaching, and to fellowship, to the breaking of bread, and to prayer."

Modern Corruption

The medieval lectionary left the church malnourished on curated pericopes. Modern topical preaching repeats the error by feeding congregations selected texts chosen for relevance, felt need, or preacher preference rather than the whole counsel of God.

expand to see more

The medieval lectionary system assembled Scripture in fragments selected for liturgical seasons and saints' days. The result was that large swaths of the biblical canon—the full Hebrew prophets, whole Pauline epistles, the wisdom literature—were never proclaimed to the medieval congregation. The Reformers identified this as spiritual starvation: the people were fed liturgical bread, but the whole loaf was kept from them. When Zwingli stood up at the Grossmünster on January 1, 1519, and announced he would begin at Matthew 1:1 and preach through the entire Gospel, the congregation heard something their grandparents never had: the whole Word of God, in order, without ecclesiastical censorship of the text.

Modern evangelical topical preaching often repeats the medieval error in a different register. Instead of liturgical seasons, the organizing principle is felt need, cultural moment, or preacher preference: a series on finances, relationships, anxiety, purpose. The texts are selected to serve the series rather than the series emerging from the text. Paul's charge to “preach the Word” in season and out of season (2 Tim 4:2)—which the lectio continua structure enforces—is bypassed in favor of preaching what the preacher or congregation wants to hear. The lectio continua is not a rigid rule but a discipline that keeps the preacher accountable to the full counsel of God rather than to their own appetites.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

From Latin lectio (reading) + continua (continuous); rooted in synagogue sequential Torah reading, recovered by the Reformation against the medieval fragmenting of Scripture.

expand to see more

Latin lectio — reading, act of reading aloud; used in the early church for the formal public reading of Scripture in worship.

Latin continua — continuous, uninterrupted, going through to completion; describes the sequential, whole-book character of the reading.

Synagogue parasháh — the weekly Torah portion; the Jewish system of continuous annual Torah readings from which the lectio continua concept descends.

Calvin's Genevan practice — the most rigorous model; his sermon series on Job, Acts, and the Epistles ran for years, shaping Geneva's congregation on the whole counsel of God.

Acts 20:27 — “I did not shrink from declaring to you the whole counsel of God”; Paul's summary of his Ephesian ministry is the theological rationale for lectio continua preaching.

Usage

"Lectio continua preaching is a discipline of submission: the preacher does not choose next Sunday's text—the canonical sequence does, which means God's Word sets the agenda, not congregational preference or pastoral comfort."

"The method forces the congregation through the hard texts as well as the beloved ones—the imprecatory psalms, the judgment oracles, the household codes—preventing a congregation from living only in their favorite passages."

"Calvin's Geneva and the Puritan tradition both practiced lectio continua as a matter of course; its recovery in Reformed and confessional churches today is a return to form, not an innovation."
